## MAC-010 — Compact source map

**Document:** IMF, *Staff Report for the 2022 Article IV Consultation—Mexico*, full report; informational annex dated **October 18, 2022**. Article IV discussions occurred **September 12–23, 2022**.  
**Extract coverage:** PDF pp. 80–104; printed report pp. 76–91 and Informational Annex pp. 2–9.  
**Source role:** International-organization staff analysis. Unless attributed to Mexican authorities or another dataset, analytical conclusions and forecasts are IMF staff assertions, not adjudicated findings. No Chapter 5B score should be derived from this extract alone.

### Atomic claims

| ID | Claim and status | Locator | 5B |
|---|---|---|---|
| C1 | **Observed/analytical:** Mexico’s inflation surge began in early 2021 and reached multi-decade highs. Food prices contributed **roughly half** of inflation above Banxico’s target-range upper limit. Only near-term expectations had risen “so far.” | p.80, Annex IX ¶¶1–2, bullets 1–2 | 5B.9 |
| C2 | **IMF interpretation:** Compared with some countries, the surge began with more economic slack and less 2020–21 macroeconomic stimulus; the unemployment gap was therefore less concerning, although manufacturing capacity utilization reached unprecedented levels. | pp.80–81, Annex IX ¶2 final bullet | 5B.9 |
| C3 | **Model-based staff estimate:** A hybrid Phillips-curve analysis attributes much of 2021–22 headline inflation through 2021Q3 to energy and food prices; residual cost-push factors added pressure, especially in 2022Q1. Robustness is described as broad, not conclusive. | p.81, Annex IX ¶3 nn.1–2 | 5B.7, 5B.9 |
| C4 | **Method qualification:** The equation was estimated over **2003–19**, omitting the volatile pandemic period, then used for a dynamic in-sample forecast for **2021Q1–2022Q2**, assuming non-lagged explanatory variables were known at end-2020. | p.81 n.1 | 5B.7 |
| C5 | **Observed balances:** Stabilization-fund transfers to the budget were **0.5% of GDP in 2019** and **0.9% in 2020**, leaving **0.2% of GDP**. Staff expected 2022 oil-revenue surprises to be insufficient for replenishment because of spending pressures. | p.83, Annex X ¶1 | 5B.3, 5B.9 |
| C6 | **Institutional fact:** Under the **Federal Budget and Fiscal Responsibility Law (FBFRL)**, FMP must transfer budgeted oil revenue to the federal government, then invest up to **2.22% and 0.64% of projected oil revenues** in federal and state stabilization funds; oil revenue above **4.7% of GDP** goes to Long-Term Reserves. | p.83, Annex X ¶2, FMP bullet | 5B.3 |
| C7 | **Expected versus prior value:** FMP federal transfers were expected at **MEX$673bn (2.3% GDP) in 2022**, versus **MEX$364bn (1.4% GDP) in 2021**. These are nominal pesos; the 2022 value is an expectation, not execution. | p.83, Annex X ¶2, FMP bullet | 5B.3 |
| C8 | **Observed/expected:** FEIP ended 2020 at **MEX$9.5bn (0.04% GDP)**, versus **MEX$158bn (0.6%)** one year earlier. It received **MEX$7.5bn (0.01%)** in 2021 and was expected to receive **MEX$8bn (0.03%)** in 2022. | pp.83–84, Annex X ¶2, FEIP bullet | 5B.3 |
| C9 | **Authorities’ estimate plus observed balance:** Authorities estimated approximately **MEX$100bn**—**0.35% of 2022 GDP / 0.33% of 2023 GDP**—as adequate 2023 contingency funding. FEIP held **MEX$25.0bn (0.09% of 2022 GDP)** at end-June 2022; staff warned the 2023 opening balance could miss the target. | p.84, Annex X ¶3 | 5B.3, 5B.9 |
| C10 | **Proposed, not enacted in extract:** The government’s 2023 budget package proposed amending the fiscal-responsibility framework so unused debt-issuance headroom would become an IOU deposited in FEIP and exchangeable in the following fiscal year. FEIP could hold liquid assets but not incur liabilities. | p.85, Annex X ¶5 and n.2 | 5B.3 |
| C11 | **Conditional forecast:** Ratification before end-2022 was expected to free **MEX$20–30bn** for FEIP. Financing remained uncertain because it depended on year-end debt-ceiling headroom. The extract does not establish ratification or execution. | pp.85–86, Annex X ¶7 | 5B.3, 5B.9 |
| C12 | **IMF assessment/recommendation:** Proposed reforms were pragmatic for near-term risks but increased complexity, weakened transparency, were unreliable, and did not correct procyclicality from the PSBR and Balanced-Budget Rule. Staff proposed a debt anchor, clearer definitions, broader expenditure-rule coverage, and medium-term sustainability planning. | pp.86–87, Annex X ¶¶7–8 and Table 1 | 5B.3 |
| C13 | **Reported reforms with attribution boundary:** Since 2019, tax-administration changes included limits on offsetting excess credits, digital-platform withholding, GAAR, merger restrictions, and OECD BEPS actions 2, 4 and 12. Staff says these reforms **may** have supported revenue performance; causal isolation is difficult. | p.90, Annex XII ¶¶1–2 | 5B.3, 5B.7 |
| C14 | **Quantified trend and authorities’ analysis:** Between 2019 and expected 2022 values, income/corporate-tax and VAT revenue rose by **1.0 and 0.6 percentage points of GDP**, respectively. Authorities’ VAT-gap analysis suggested approximately **MEX$170bn** less evasion during 2018–21; IMF staff does not independently establish causality. | p.90, Annex XII ¶2 | 5B.3, 5B.7 |
| C15 | **Data-quality assessment:** IMF judged data timely and adequate for surveillance and the 2021 ROSC called national accounts high quality, but identified cash-versus-accrual recording, public-sector reconciliation, subnational coverage, partial pension-liability reporting, face-value debt reporting, and omitted Banxico liquidity-management T-bonds. | pp.97, 100–101, Fund Relations ¶2; Statistical Issues §§National accounts–Government finance | 5B.7 |
| C16 | **Contrary qualification:** Financial Soundness Indicator publication was interrupted after May 2021 for IFRS9 revisions; authorities supplied old-standard updates on request. External statistics were high quality, but external-debt coverage, valuation, accrual treatment, and cross-dataset consistency remained incomplete. | p.101, §§Financial-sector surveillance–ESS | 5B.7 |
| C17 | **Program-status fact:** As of August 31, 2022, Mexico had no outstanding IMF purchases or loans. Its Nov. 19, 2021–Nov. 18, 2023 Flexible Credit Line approved **SDR 35,650.80m**, with **SDR 0 drawn**. No conditionality or reform target tied to drawings appears in this extract. | pp.97–98, Fund Relations tables | 5B.3 |

### Limitations and reopen list

- Extract excludes the report’s main macro tables, staff appraisal, authorities’ views, debt-sustainability analysis, and headline growth/fiscal/debt/reserve forecasts; reopen these before broader conclusions.
- **Reopen Annex X against enacted 2022 legislation** to verify amendment name, final text, passage date, effective date, exceptions, and implementation.
- Recheck chart values on pp.80–82 against original PDF graphics; OCR does not reliably preserve axes or series.
- Reopen pension Annex XIII for distributional and fiscal effects (pp.91–92): several effects are explicitly forecasts or possibilities, not outcomes.
- Reconcile narrative fiscal values with report tables and SHCP outturns; this extract mixes observed, expected, and authority-estimated figures.
